name: Canrenone

lead: Canrenone is a steroid-based drug in the spirolactone family and one of the active breakdown products (metabolites) of spironolactone. Appearance interest comes from spironolactone, which clinicians prescribe off-label for hormonal acne and female pattern hair loss because it blocks androgen effects. Canrenone shares part of that activity.

It is used medically as a diuretic and in heart failure research, mainly in Italy and some other countries via its potassium salt. Reference sources describe it as considerably weaker than spironolactone as an antiandrogen, and no published trials test it for acne or hair.

paras: Canrenone is not sold as a skin or hair product. Where available, it is a prescription medicine for fluid retention and heart conditions. People interested in anti-androgen skin or hair routes typically discuss spironolactone with a clinician, in which canrenone forms inside the body.

As a mineralocorticoid blocker it can raise blood potassium and affects kidney function; gynecomastia is among the endpoints tracked in heart-failure reviews. Reviews of this drug class also examine effects on blood sugar. Use is prescription-only and monitored by clinicians.

angle.text: Canrenone matters to appearance mostly as a piece of spironolactone's pharmacology. On its own it is a prescription diuretic and not a skin or hair treatment.

lead: Canrenone is a steroidal antimineralocorticoid of the spirolactone class and an active metabolite of spironolactone, meaning the body produces it from spironolactone and it contributes to that drug's effects.[1] It was described in 1959, and its potassium salt, potassium canrenoate, entered medical use in 1968.[1]

Its link to appearance is indirect. Spironolactone is prescribed by clinicians off-label for hormonal acne and hair thinning because it opposes androgens, and canrenone is part of the same pharmacology. Reference sources state that canrenone is considerably less potent and effective as an antiandrogen than spironolactone, though it has been reported useful for hirsutism in women.[1]

Canrenone itself is used as a diuretic in some European countries, and trials have studied it in heart failure, hypertension and metabolic syndrome.[2][3][4] No human studies of canrenone for skin or hair appearance are known.
infobox: Prescription; reported to remain marketed in Italy, potassium canrenoate elsewhere

paras: Canrenone and potassium canrenoate are used as diuretics, and studies have examined them in heart failure and hypertension.[1][2][3] A network meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials found spironolactone and eplerenone reduced all-cause mortality in chronic heart failure, while no conclusion could be drawn for canrenone because of the small evidence base.[5]

Canrenone is not marketed for acne or hair. Its relevance comes from spironolactone's off-label dermatologic use. Reference sources note it is reported effective for hirsutism in women and is a less potent antiandrogen than spironolactone.[1]

Canrenone blocks mineralocorticoid receptors and is reported as more potent than spironolactone at that job, though another spironolactone metabolite accounts for most of the potassium-sparing effect. It also inhibits some steroid-making enzymes, less strongly than spironolactone, is about 95 percent protein bound, and has a half-life of about 16.5 hours.[1] Reviews describe mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists as a class with differing pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics.[6]

Class-wide concerns include high blood potassium, acute kidney injury and gynecomastia, which network meta-analyses track as safety endpoints.[5] A systematic review of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, including canrenone, found heterogeneous glucose effects that appeared to depend on the disease studied.[7]

Randomized trials have tested canrenone in mild chronic heart failure, in hypertensive type 2 diabetes against hydrochlorothiazide, and on inflammatory markers in metabolic syndrome.[2][3][4] A 1976 trial in healthy volunteers found potassium canrenoate less potent than spironolactone on a weight or molar basis.[8] No trials have studied canrenone for acne or hair loss.

timeline.event: Potassium canrenoate introduced for medical use.[1]
